[[File:IMO logo.svg|thumb|right|alt=A circle, interlinked with a sideways figure of eight (lemniscate). The circle is half green and half yellow, the lemniscate is a third red, a third blue and a third black. The shapes are featured in front of a white background.|Logo of the International Mathematical Olympiad]]
The first of the [[International Mathematical Olympiad]]s (IMOs) was held in [[Socialist Republic of Romania|Romania]] in 1959. The oldest of the [[International Science Olympiad]]s, the IMO has since been held annually, except in 1980. That year, the competition initially planned to be held in [[Mongolia]] was cancelled due to the [[Soviet invasion of Afghanistan]].<ref name=Mongolia/> Because the competition was initially founded for [[Eastern Europe]]an countries participating in the [[Warsaw Pact]], under the influence of the [[Eastern Bloc]],<ref name="more">{{cite web|url=http://imo.wolfram.com/morefacts.html|title=More IMO Facts|access-date=2008-03-05|archive-date=2001-08-20|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20010820012443/http://imo.wolfram.com/morefacts.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> the earlier IMOs were hosted only in Eastern European countries, gradually spreading to other nations.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://sms.math.nus.edu.sg/Simo/Simo.aspx|title=Singapore International Mathematical Olympiad (SIMO) Home Page|access-date=2008-02-04|publisher=Singapore Mathematical Society|archive-date=2003-03-27|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030327035236/http://sms.math.nus.edu.sg/Simo/Simo.aspx|url-status=dead}}</ref>

The first IMO was held in [[Socialist Republic of Romania|Romania]] in 1959. Seven countries entered &ndash; [[Bulgaria]], [[Czechoslovakia]], [[East Germany]], [[Hungary]], [[Poland]], Romania and the [[Soviet Union]] &ndash; with the hosts finishing as the top-ranked nation.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.imo-official.org/year_country_r.aspx?year=1959|title=1st IMO 1959|access-date=2011-06-20|publisher=International Mathematical Olympiad|archive-date=2011-09-25|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110925081933/http://www.imo-official.org/year_country_r.aspx?year=1959|url-status=live}}</ref> The number of participating countries has since risen: 14 countries took part in 1969, 50 in 1989, and 104 in 2009.<ref name=timeline>{{cite web|url=http://www.imo-official.org/organizers.aspx|title=Timeline|access-date=2011-06-20|publisher=International Mathematical Olympiad|archive-date=2007-10-11|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071011202734/http://www.imo-official.org/organizers.aspx|url-status=live}}</ref>

[[North Korea]] is the only country whose entire team has been caught cheating, resulting in its disqualification at the 32nd IMO in 1991 and the 51st IMO in 2010.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.imo-official.org/country_team_r.aspx?code=PRK|title=International Mathematical Olympiad: Democratic People's Republic of Korea|access-date=2010-07-17|archive-date=2007-10-12|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071012005302/http://www.imo-official.org/country_team_r.aspx?code=PRK|url-status=live}}</ref> (However, the 2010 case was controversial.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.imo-register.org.uk/2010-report.html|title=International Mathematical Olympiad 2010 UK leader's report, Almaty and Astana, Kazakhstan|author=Geoff Smith|website=UK IMO Register|access-date=2023-09-06|archive-date=2023-09-04|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230904234216/https://www.imo-register.org.uk/2010-report.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6h357005|title=North Korea's disqualification at IMO 2010.|website=Art of Problem Solving|access-date=2023-09-06|archive-date=2023-10-21|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231021084003/https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6h357005|url-status=live}}</ref>) There have been other disqualifications of contestants due to cheating, but such cases are not officially made public.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.imo-register.org.uk/1993-report.html|title=34th International Mathematical Olympiad, Istanbul, Turkey, UK leader's report|author=Adam McBride|website=UK IMO Register|access-date=2023-11-24|archive-date=2023-09-04|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230904234225/https://www.imo-register.org.uk/1993-report.html|url-status=live}}</ref> In January 2011, [[Google]] gave €1 million to the IMO organization to help cover the costs of the events from 2011 to 2015.<ref>[http://googlepolicyeurope.blogspot.com/2011/01/giving-young-mathematicians-chance-to.html Google Europe Blog: Giving young mathematicians the chance to shine] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160308031218/http://googlepolicyeurope.blogspot.com/2011/01/giving-young-mathematicians-chance-to.html |date=2016-03-08 }}. Googlepolicyeurope.blogspot.com (2011-01-21). Retrieved on 2013-10-29.</ref>

!scope=row|''{{flagicon|RUS}}'' [[Saint Petersburg|St. Petersburg]] (online){{#tag:ref|Following the [[COVID-19 pandemic]], the 2020 IMO was postponed from July to September hoping to keep the competition in-person. Then it was changed to a virtual event.<ref name="virtual2020">{{cite web|url=https://imof.co/virtual-imo2020-in-st-petersburg/|title=Virtual IMO 2020 – Russia|website=International Mathematical Olympiad Foundation|date=2020-07-11|access-date=2022-07-16|archive-date=2023-06-09|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230609172038/https://imof.co/virtual-imo2020-in-st-petersburg/|url-status=live}}</ref>|group=n}}{{#tag:ref|For the two virtual IMOs, all problems were selected by the Problem Selection Committee instead of the Jury made up of all team leaders, and problems were sent to the team leaders shortly before the exams for translation. Each team took the IMO exam at a national exam centre, and starting times of all exams were in the interval between 07:30 and 12:00 UTC (both ends included) of each exam day.
